meta.about: Apollo Hospitals was established in 1983 by Dr. Prathap C Reddy, renowned architect of modern healthcare in India. As the nation’s first corporate hospital, Apollo Hospitals is acclaimed for pioneering the private healthcare revolution in the country. Apollo Hospitals has emerged as Asia’s foremost integrated healthcare services provider and has a robust presence across the healthcare ecosystem, including Hospitals, Pharmacies, Primary Care & Diagnostic Clinics and several Retail Health models. [1]
meta.keyPoints: Business Segments: a) Healthcare Services (50% in FY26 vs 55% in FY22):[1][2][3] The company has a capacity of 10,970 beds in 78 hospitals located in India and overseas, out of which 9,481 beds are located in 49 owned hospitals, 699 beds in Day Surgery & Cradles and 790 beds are in 6 managed hospitals. b) Digital Health & Pharmacy Distribution (43% in FY26 vs 37% in FY22):[4] The WOS Apollo HealthCo (AHL) manages India’s largest organized pharmacy network, operating across 22 states and 5 union territories, with a presence in 1,200 cities and towns. It has 7,289 active stores. Sales from its offline private and generic labels contribute 15.3% of the total revenue (Q4FY26). Additionally, its online platform, Apollo 24x7, has over 47 million registered users and 9 lakh daily active users.[5] c) Retail Health & Diagnostics (7% in FY26 vs 8% in FY22):[6] The WOS Apollo Health & Lifestyle operates 2,501 diagnostics centers, 167 dialysis centers, 280 dental centers, and 316 clinics. As of FY26, the segment has a footfall of 33,461 per day and an average gross realization per patient of Rs. 1,608.[7]

profile.text: India's largest private hospital group: 48 owned hospitals plus 6 managed, 9,857 census beds in its network (owned, managed and AHLL; 11,147 capacity) and 8,352 operating beds incl. the 22%-owned Delhi hospital (Jun-2026). Three reported businesses: Healthcare Services (hospitals, 50% of FY26 revenue and 81% of EBITDA), Apollo HealthCo (pharmacy distribution to ~7,440 Apollo pharmacies plus the Apollo 24/7 digital platform, 43% of revenue) and Apollo Health & Lifestyle (AHLL: clinics, diagnostics, Spectra day surgery, dialysis, Cradle and fertility, 7%). Founded in 1983 by Dr Prathap C. Reddy (first hospital in Chennai); the Reddy family owns 28%.

segments.note: Q1FY27 network: 299 clinics, 172 dialysis centres, 294 dental centres, ~2,894 diagnostic collection points. Diagnostics revenue +31% and EBITDA +136% in Q1FY27; management targets 20%+ growth and ~20% diagnostics margin within 6-8 quarters. AHLL became 100% owned in Mar-2026 (Rs1,273 cr paid to IFC and other minorities).

callPoints: Hospital revenue growth of ~20% in FY27 'on track' (MD); 18-20% for the year (CFO). Established hospitals to grow 13-14% a year (7-8% volume) and new hospitals to add ~7% over the next 24 months.
Established-hospital margin of ~26% is 'a good sustainable number' (CFO); margins to 'inch up a bit' over 24 months.

New-hospital losses ~Rs150 cr for FY27, rising by ~Rs20 cr a quarter when Gurgaon opens (soft launch Sep-2026, opening Oct-2026, revenue from Q4FY27); Hyderabad Financial District to break even in Q2FY27; the new-hospital cluster to break even by Q3-Q4 FY28.
Pricing: ~5% a year ('medical inflation'); insurance contracts reset every two years. 70% of patients pay under Rs2 lakh per admission.
Bangladesh in-patient volumes back to 60-70% of their peak; international revenue +26%.
Digital (24/7) cash breakeven expected in Q2FY27; insurance broking breakeven by end-Q3FY27; steady-state 24/7 cost ~Rs80 cr a quarter.
Payer mix: cash + insurance at ~85% 'very maintained' even outside the South.
MD on the Parliamentary committee's pricing recommendations: price controls 'may dis-incentivise investments'; tariff increases mirror inflation.

restructuring.text: Composite scheme (announced end-Jun-2025): Apollo's omni-channel pharmacy distribution and Apollo 24/7 (its shares in Apollo HealthCo) and the AHEL telehealth division are demerged into a new company (Apollo Healthtech Ltd); Apollo HealthCo and Keimed (the promoter-linked pharmaceutical wholesaler) then merge into it. AHEL shareholders receive 195.2 NewCo shares per 100 AHEL shares. Resulting NewCo: AHEL shareholders 42.1% directly, AHEL 15% plus ~2.5% economic interest through its 49% stake in FHPL (so 59.6% for AHEL and its shareholders combined), Advent 12.1%, ESOP 3.0%, Keimed promoters and others 25.3%. NewCo owns 25.5% of AMPL, holding company of the Apollo Pharmacies store chain. NCLT Chennai convened the meetings (order of 26-Mar-2026); shareholders approved the scheme on 24-Jun-2026; final NCLT sanction and listing are pending, with listing estimated by Q4FY27 'post all approvals'. Advent International invested Rs2,475 cr in Apollo HealthCo through CCPS (Sep-2024 and Mar-2025); the CCPS sit in consolidated borrowings (Rs2,457 cr at Mar-26) and convert when the scheme takes effect. The proceeds funded purchases of Keimed shares (Rs800 cr at fair value in investments, Mar-26).

cloudnine.text: AHLL is combining Apollo Cradle and Apollo Fertility with Cloudnine (Kids Clinic India Ltd): valued at ~Rs1,550 cr (~35x FY26 IGAAP EBITDA of Rs45 cr on Rs450 cr revenue), paid in cash (~Rs750 cr, to be redeployed in primary care) and a 9.9% fully diluted stake in Cloudnine. Announced 20-May-2026; CCI approved on 1-Sep-2026; management expected completion in Q2FY27.

accounting.indAs116: EBITDA is post-Ind AS 116: lease rent (Rs85 cr in Q1FY27, ~Rs291 cr of lease payments in FY26) is excluded and shows up as right-of-use depreciation and lease interest (Rs174 cr of lease finance cost in FY26). Lease liabilities Rs2,834 cr (Mar-26), Rs2,877 cr (Jun-26).
accounting.ccps: Advent's CCPS in Apollo HealthCo (Rs2,457 cr) are classified entirely as a liability (equity component negligible) and as current, as management expects conversion within a year.
accounting.esop: HealthCo ESOP charges (Rs118 cr in FY26, Rs10 cr in Q1FY27) are inside EBITDA; group share-based pay was Rs159 cr in FY26.
accounting.delhi: The Delhi hospital (Indraprastha Medical Corporation, 22.03%, listed) is an associate: its beds and patients are in the KPIs but only its profit share is in the accounts.

regulatory.text: The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health (176th report, laid on 7-Aug-2026) recommended benchmarking private-hospital room charges in metros to nearby three-star hotel tariffs, ending room-category-linked pricing of procedures, standard package rates, mandatory cost estimates and an independent regulator. Hospital stocks fell up to 3%. These are recommendations, not law; such changes typically take 1-2 years if adopted.

assumptions._note: GAM Research forecast drivers for Apollo Hospitals (consolidated, Rs crore). Built by reported business: Healthcare Services (hospitals), Apollo HealthCo (pharmacy distribution + Apollo 24/7) and AHLL; group EBITDA = sum of the three (post-Ind AS 116, as reported). The hospital revenue path comes from a bed build (beds x occupancy / ALOS x revenue per in-patient) kept in `businessLines` and checked against model revenue in APOLLOHOSP.ctx.js. Profit is attributable to owners (APOLLOHOSP.patch.js); the tax line carries tax plus minorities. Screener 'borrowings' include lease liabilities and Advent's CCPS in Apollo HealthCo, so the model's net cash is net of both; the SOTP adds the CCPS back (Advent's claim sits in the 40.4% of NewCo not owned by Apollo's shareholders). Valued on sum of the parts, as the street does.

segments.name: Healthcare Services (hospitals)
segments._why: From the bed build in businessLines.hcs: average operating beds 8,600 / 9,250 / 9,550 (Jun-26: 8,352; +620 commissioned beds over 12-18 months, Gurgaon 380 census beds from Oct-2026, 327 brownfield beds in FY28-29), occupancy 69% / 69.5% / 70.5% (Q1FY27 70%, established 72%; new beds dilute), ALOS 3.10 / 3.05 / 3.02 days, revenue per in-patient +7.6% / +7.0% / +6.5% (~5% price + case mix; +8% in Q1FY27). FY27 +19.5% sits inside management's 18-20%; FY28 +17.8% (guidance: 13-14% established + ~7% new over 24 months); FY29 +12.7% as few beds open before the FY30-31 greenfields.
segments._marginWhy: FY26 24.4%, Q1FY27 24.2% (established 25.9%, new hospitals -Rs38 cr). FY27 23.8%: established ~26% on ~Rs14,250 cr less ~Rs175 cr of new-hospital losses (guided ~Rs150 cr, rising ~Rs20 cr a quarter with Gurgaon). FY28 24.1%: new cluster breaks even by Q3-Q4 FY28. FY29 24.7%: established inching up (management), new units profitable, early pre-opening costs for the FY30-31 greenfields.

segments.name: Apollo HealthCo (pharmacy distribution + 24/7)
segments._why: FY26 +19%, Q1FY27 +20% (+22% excluding an exited corporate partner); offline distribution +22%, digital pharmacy and diagnostics +25-30%. 19% / 17% / 16%: store additions (~7,440 stores) and private label, slowing as the base grows.
segments._marginWhy: EBITDA after the 24/7 operating cost and ESOP charge (reported basis): FY25 1.8%, FY26 4.5%, Q1FY27 5.8%. Before digital costs the margin is ~8.8%; 24/7 costs ~Rs80 cr a quarter (guided steady), ESOP ~Rs40 cr in FY27. 6.0% / 6.8% / 7.2% assumes digital breakeven in FY27 and pre-digital margin of 8.9-9.1%, below the ~6.5-7% guided for the combined NewCo exit run-rate once Keimed's ~3% margin is blended in, i.e. we assume slower margin gains than management.

segments.name: AHLL (clinics, diagnostics, specialty care)
segments._why: Apollo Cradle and Fertility (Rs450 cr revenue in FY26) leave for Cloudnine; CCI approved on 1-Sep-2026 and management expected completion in Q2FY27, so we deconsolidate from Q3FY27. Continuing AHLL (~Rs1,415 cr in FY26) grows ~18% a year (diagnostics +31% in Q1FY27, primary care +12%): FY27 Rs1,889 cr (+1%, half a year of Cradle), FY28 Rs1,968 cr (+4%), FY29 +17%.
segments._marginWhy: FY26 11.4% (incl. Cradle/Fertility, ~Rs45 cr IGAAP EBITDA); Q1FY27 11.8%. Diagnostics margin 14% in Q1FY27, targeted ~20% within 6-8 quarters. 12.2% / 13.5% / 14.5%.

assumptions._unallocLabel: Corporate costs not in any segment
assumptions._unallocWhy: Segments sum to consolidated EBITDA as reported (FY26 Rs3,769 cr; Screener shows Rs3,779 cr after a Rs10 cr reclassification).

businessLines._why: Hospital revenue build (network KPIs include the 22%-owned Delhi hospital, as the company reports them). discharges = average operating beds x occupancy x 365 / ALOS; in-patient revenue = discharges x average revenue per in-patient (ARPP); network net revenue = in-patient revenue / in-patient share (81.7% in FY26: 628,998 x Rs178,434 = Rs11,224 cr of Rs13,740 cr); consolidated hospital revenue = network revenue x 91.4% (FY26 Rs12,555 cr of Rs13,740 cr; Q1FY27 91.7%), removing Delhi. Average beds 8,600 / 9,250 / 9,550 (FY26 average ~8,070; Jun-26 8,352); FY26 calibrates to 67.7% occupancy on average beds (reported 67%).

assumptions._capexWhy: Cash capex ~Rs2,200 / 2,200 / 2,300 cr plus new leases (right-of-use additions, Rs203 cr in FY26 and Rs522 cr in FY25) ~Rs250 cr a year, because the model's net debt includes lease liabilities. Cash capex = ~Rs550 cr recurring hospital capex (management) + ~Rs1,500 cr a year of the Rs7,500 cr still to be spent on the FY31 bed plan + ~Rs150 cr for HealthCo and AHLL. FY26 capex Rs1,962 cr (Screener).
assumptions._depWhy: FY26 depreciation Rs876 cr (incl. right-of-use) = 5.1% of average gross block (Rs17,220 cr); Q1FY27 Rs235 cr (Rs940 cr annualised). 5.0% gives FY27E ~Rs975 cr with Gurgaon opening; the engine depreciates capex at once while projects sit in CWIP.
assumptions._treasuryWhy: Zero because the engine would apply it to net cash after lease liabilities and CCPS, which is negative. Treasury income is built on gross treasury in `otherIncome`.
assumptions._otherIncomeWhy: Built from AR FY26 note 32 and note 10 (Screener's other income also carries the share of associates). (1) Treasury income: FY26 Rs139 cr (bank deposits Rs53.7 cr + mutual-fund fair-value gains Rs62.5 cr + gains on financial assets Rs22.8 cr) on ~Rs2,600 cr average treasury = ~5.3%. We take 5.5% on opening company treasury of Rs2,336 / 2,350 / 2,300 cr (capex absorbs free cash; ~Rs750 cr of Cloudnine cash arrives in FY27) = Rs128 / 129 / 127 cr. (2) Recurring other items: interest on other financial assets Rs20.3 cr, dividends Rs2.7 cr, miscellaneous Rs26.7 cr, write-backs Rs1.0 cr = ~Rs45-50 cr. (3) Share of associates (Delhi hospital, FHPL and others): Rs44.9 cr in FY26, Rs13.4 cr in Q1FY27 -> Rs52 / 58 / 64 cr. Total Rs225 / 235 / 240 cr vs FY26 Rs236.5 cr like-for-like (Screener Rs207 cr after the Rs19 cr labour-code exceptional and a Rs10 cr reclassification) and Rs231 cr in the twelve months to Jun-26. One-offs left out: PPE disposal gain Rs1.9 cr.

otherTreasury._why: Bank deposits over 12 months inside other financial assets (Rs174 cr non-current + Rs28 cr current, AR FY26 note 14), not in Screener's cash or investments; with them Screener cash (Rs1,117 cr) and mutual funds (Rs1,017 cr) give the company's Rs2,336 cr of cash and treasury.

assumptions._interestLabel: Finance cost (bank debt, lease interest, CCPS)
assumptions._interestWhy: FY26 Rs450 cr (lease interest Rs174 cr); Q1FY27 Rs120 cr (Rs482 cr annualised). Gross bank debt Rs3,244 cr and leases Rs2,877 cr at Jun-26; new leases and capex funding add ~Rs25 cr a year.
assumptions._taxWhy: Tax plus minorities (engine workaround: there is no minority line). FY26: PBT Rs2,661 cr, tax Rs658 cr (24.7%), minorities Rs61 cr, attributable PAT Rs1,942 cr = 27.0% leakage. Q1FY27: PBT Rs799 cr, tax Rs188 cr (23.6%), minorities Rs30 cr = 27.3%. We take 24.5% tax + ~3.2% minorities (Assam, Lucknow, Ahmedabad, Imperial and others; Rs110-130 cr a year).
assumptions._payoutWhy: FY26 dividend Rs20 a share (Rs288 cr) = 15% of EPS; capex absorbs the rest.

dcf._betaWhy: Net debt incl. leases but excl. CCPS is ~Rs3,600 cr, ~3% of enterprise value, so WACC is close to the 11.6% cost of equity the engine uses (beta 0.85: defensive demand, but regulatory and execution risk).
dcf._tgWhy: Healthcare spending grows faster than nominal GDP as insurance spreads; 6% nominal, the top of the house range.
dcf._fadeGrowthWhy: Revenue growth fades from ~15% to 9% by year 15 as the bed plan completes and pharmacy matures.
dcf._fadeMarginWhy: 17.5% consolidated: hospitals ~25% and pharmacy ~7.5% at a roughly even revenue mix, plus AHLL.
dcf._fadeCapexWhy: Capex fades from ~6.5% of revenue to 5.5% (replacement ~3.8% plus growth beds); FY26 7.8%.

bull.label: Bull
bull.narrative: Gurgaon and the new hospitals fill a year early, price increases stick (no regulatory caps), established margins move to 27%, HealthCo hits the guided 7% NewCo margin in FY28 and NewCo lists at pharmacy-retail multiples.

bear.label: Bear
bear.narrative: The Parliamentary panel's pricing ideas turn into room-rent and package caps, new hospitals in the North and West ramp slowly, digital losses persist, and the market pays mid-cycle multiples for hospitals and a distribution multiple for NewCo.

cover.headline: India's best hospital franchise at a fair price: the hospitals justify today's value, but there is little left over for the pharmacy spin-off
cover.lead: Apollo runs India's largest private hospital network (48 owned and 6 managed hospitals, ~10,000 census beds), supplies ~7,440 Apollo pharmacies through Apollo HealthCo, and owns clinics and diagnostics (AHLL). Hospitals are the engine: occupancy rose to 70% in Q1FY27, revenue per in-patient grew 8%, and established hospitals earn a 25.9% EBITDA margin. The pharmacy and digital arm is being spun off: after a scheme approved by shareholders in Jun-2026, Apollo's shareholders will own **59.6%** of a listed NewCo that also absorbs Keimed, a promoter-linked wholesaler. The street values Apollo on a **sum of the parts (SOTP)**, hospitals at 26-30x EV/EBITDA. We forecast EBITDA of ₹4,574 / 5,549 / 6,511 cr and EPS of ₹167.7 / 209.8 / 250.8 for FY27-29E, below the street. Valuing hospitals at **24x Sep-28E EBITDA**, NewCo at 18x (Apollo's 59.6%), AHLL at 18x, and deducting minorities the street ignores gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}})**: **we initiate with HOLD.** Cross-checks: P/E ₹10,364, DCF ₹5,660. Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: The best hospital franchise in India, getting better
arguments.p: Q1FY27: in-patient volumes +13%, occupancy 70% (65% a year earlier), revenue per in-patient ₹1,86,630 (+8%), hospital ROCE 28.5%. Cardiac, oncology, transplant, neuro, gastro and ortho are 62% of in-patient revenue; self-pay and insurance ~85% of in-patient revenue. We model group revenue +{{F.salesGrowth.0|pct}} in FY27, with hospitals +19.5% from a bed-by-bed build.

arguments.h: A bigger bed plan, and harder markets
arguments.p: Census beds go from 9,857 to ~14,100 by FY31 (+4,330) for ~₹11,150 cr, with ~₹7,500 cr still to spend; most new beds are in the North and West (Gurgaon from Oct-2026, then Worli, Dwarka, Varanasi, Ranchi), where Apollo's record is weaker (West occupancy 58%). New hospitals lose ~₹150 cr in FY27; we hold the hospital margin at 23.8-24.7% (FY27-29E).

Apollo 24/7 ran up ~₹2,100 cr of operating costs over FY23-26; its cash loss was down to ₹10 cr in Q1FY27. NewCo (pharmacy distribution, 24/7, Keimed) targets ₹25,000 cr of annualised revenue at a 6.5-7% EBITDA margin by Q4FY27 and listing by Q4FY27. But it is a distribution business, and Advent (12.1%) and Keimed's owners (25.3%) share it; we value Apollo's 59.6% at ~₹1,376 a share.

At ₹8,166 the market pays ~20.8x our Sep-28E hospital EBITDA once the other parts are valued, against our derived 24x (Apollo's 25.4x forward median since 2021, less the ~7% hospital-sector de-rating). The street's higher targets (avg ~₹10,110 after Q1) use 26-30x and deduct nothing for minorities (~₹267 a share). The Parliamentary panel's pricing ideas are the main threat to the multiple.

sections.title: Three businesses in one stock: hospitals that earn the money, a pharmacy arm that turns it over, clinics that feed both

blocks.p: **Healthcare Services (hospitals)** is half of revenue and four-fifths of EBITDA: ₹12,555 cr of revenue and ₹3,069 cr of EBITDA (24.4%) in FY26. The network had 8,352 operating beds in Jun-2026 (6 metros 4,848 beds at 72% occupancy and ₹2.23 lakh per in-patient; 18 smaller cities 3,504 beds at 66% and ₹1.32 lakh). The Delhi hospital (Indraprastha, 22% owned, listed) is in the bed counts but only its profit share is consolidated. Apollo is a tertiary-care chain: cardiac, oncology (incl. a proton-therapy centre in Chennai), transplants, neurosciences, gastro and orthopaedics ("CONGO-T") are 62% of in-patient revenue; 6% comes from international patients from ~150 countries.

**Apollo HealthCo** (₹10,808 cr revenue, ₹488 cr EBITDA after digital costs in FY26) buys medicines and supplies the ~7,440 Apollo pharmacies, which are owned by Apollo Medicals (AMPL, an associate) rather than by Apollo itself; it also runs private-label products (15.2% of sales) and **Apollo 24/7**, the app (49 mn registered users) for teleconsults, medicine delivery, diagnostics booking and insurance. Before digital costs it earns ~8.8%; after the ₹349 cr of 24/7 operating cost and ₹118 cr of ESOP charges in FY26, 4.5%. **AHLL** (₹1,865 cr, 11.4% margin) runs 299 clinics, diagnostics (₹706 cr of revenue in FY26), Spectra day-surgery centres, dialysis and dental chains, and (until the Cloudnine deal completes) Cradle maternity and fertility centres.

sections.title: Too few good beds, and a regulator starting to look at prices

blocks.p: India spends little on healthcare and has few hospital beds (government beds ~0.79 per 1,000 people), so demand for quality private tertiary care keeps outrunning supply. Antique estimates healthcare delivery grows 10-12% a year to ~₹12 lakh cr by FY30, with private providers' share of treatments rising from 64% to ~69%. The listed chains are responding with the biggest building programme in their history: ~19,000 beds added in FY23-26 and plans for +54% more (to ~108,000) by FY30, two-thirds brownfield. Insurance is the fastest-growing payer and now negotiates hard, resetting tariffs every two years. Pricing is also becoming political: on 7-Aug-2026 a Parliamentary committee recommended linking metro room charges to three-star hotel rates, ending room-linked pricing of procedures and creating a hospital-price regulator.

sections.title: Hospital revenue = beds × occupancy × patients × price: for four years Apollo grew on occupancy and price, not beds

blocks.p: Apollo reports its hospitals as a network that includes the 22%-owned Delhi hospital: **operating beds**, **occupancy**, **in-patient discharges**, **average length of stay (ALOS)** and **average revenue per in-patient (ARPP)**. Discharges × ARPP gives in-patient revenue (~82% of the network's net revenue; the rest is out-patients and other services), and the consolidated hospital segment is ~91% of network revenue (the gap is mainly Delhi). From FY22 to FY26 operating beds rose only 3% (7,875 → 8,131), but occupancy rose from 63% to 67% (70% in Q1FY27), stays fell from 3.96 to 3.17 days (so each bed treated more patients), and ARPP rose 25% (₹1.43 lakh → ₹1.78 lakh) on price (~4-5% a year) and sicker, more complex cases. Revenue per occupied bed-day (ARPP ÷ ALOS) was ₹56,288 in FY26 and ₹60,398 in Q1FY27.

sections.title: Apollo HealthCo: the digital bleed has stopped; now the spin-off decides who keeps the value

blocks.p: HealthCo grew revenue 19% in FY26 and 20% in Q1FY27 (₹2,977 cr). Its offline distribution business earns ~7.3% EBITDA; the online pharmacy and 24/7 platform earn ~20% before the platform's operating cost (₹81 cr in Q1FY27), and the "digital cash loss" fell from ₹49 cr in Q1FY26 to ₹10 cr in Q1FY27, with breakeven guided for Q2FY27. Apollo shareholders get 195.2 NewCo shares per 100 Apollo shares (42.1% of NewCo) and Apollo keeps 15% plus ~2.5% through FHPL: **59.6% in all**. Advent (which put ₹2,475 cr into HealthCo in 2024-25) gets 12.1%, ESOPs 3.0%, Keimed's owners 25.3%. NCLT sanction is pending; listing is estimated by Q4FY27.

verdicts: 40-year brand; 150 countries send patients; transplant, oncology (proton) and cardiac programmes; Chennai children's hospital in Newsweek's list.
Largest network (~10,000 census beds); dense in Chennai (11 hospitals), Hyderabad (8), Bengaluru (10) and Kolkata; weaker in Mumbai (58% occupancy in the West) and the North.
ARPP +8% in Q1FY27 (price +4%), but 46% of revenue now comes from insurers who negotiate, and a Parliamentary panel wants caps.
Referral funnel and 49 mn app users; but the digital arm burned ~₹2,000 cr of operating cost in FY23-26 and is only now breaking even.

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** Apollo has the strongest hospital brand in India and genuine clinical depth (transplants, oncology, proton therapy, complex cardiac care), which lets it charge the highest prices per patient in its markets and attract international patients. That moat is deepest where Apollo has density (Chennai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Kolkata). It is not a moat against regulation or against well-funded rivals in Delhi NCR and Mumbai, where Max, Medanta and Fortis are strong and where most of Apollo's new beds go. The pharmacy and digital ecosystem is a feeder, not a moat: it cost ~₹2,100 cr of operating spend to build and is now being shared with Advent and Keimed's owners.

sections.title: Revenue up 2.2x since FY20 and margins at a decade high, because the digital losses finally shrank

blocks.p: Apollo's revenue grew from ₹11,247 cr in FY20 to ₹25,228 cr in FY26 (14% a year). Covid cut FY21 by 6%; FY22 jumped 39% on the recovery, Covid testing and vaccination, and the new pharmacy-distribution structure. Since then growth has been a steady 13-16% a year. The margin story is the digital platform: Apollo 24/7 cost ₹619-657 cr a year in FY23-24 and pushed the group EBITDA margin down to ~12.5%; as those costs fell (₹349 cr in FY26) and hospital margins held at ~24%, the group margin rose to 15.0% in FY26 and 15.5% in Q1FY27. Profit attributable to shareholders went from ₹819 cr (FY23) to ₹1,942 cr (FY26), 33% a year.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean audit, but four things distort the headline numbers

bullets: **Leases (Ind AS 116).** EBITDA is post-Ind AS 116: lease rent (₹85 cr in Q1FY27, ~₹291 cr of lease payments in FY26) is excluded and shows up as right-of-use depreciation and lease interest (₹174 cr of lease finance cost in FY26). Lease liabilities ₹2,834 cr (Mar-26), ₹2,877 cr (Jun-26). Pre-Ind AS (after rent) the FY26 EBITDA margin was ~13.8%, not 15.0%. We value on post-Ind AS EBITDA and count lease liabilities as debt, consistently.

**Advent's CCPS.** Advent's CCPS in Apollo HealthCo (₹2,457 cr) are classified entirely as a liability (equity component negligible) and as current, as management expects conversion within a year. It inflates Screener's debt by ₹2,457 cr; we add it back in the SOTP because Advent's claim is in the 40.4% of NewCo we do not value.

**Minorities.** Profit to minorities was ₹61 cr in FY26 (Assam ₹23 cr, Lucknow ₹20 cr, Ahmedabad ₹12 cr, Imperial ₹9 cr) and ₹30 cr in Q1FY27 alone. Screener's "net profit" is before them; we use profit attributable to shareholders and deduct the minorities' share of value.
**Restated quarters.** Screener now shows Q2FY26 and Q1FY27 revenue lower than first published (₹6,189 cr and ₹6,932 cr vs ₹6,303.5 cr and ₹7,043.5 cr); we use the figures published by 30-Sep-2026.

**ESOPs and one-offs.** HealthCo ESOP charges (₹118 cr in FY26, ₹10 cr in Q1FY27) are inside EBITDA; group share-based pay was ₹159 cr in FY26. FY26 had a ₹19 cr labour-code provision (exceptional); FY22 had ₹220 cr of exceptional gains. Other income (₹237 cr in FY26 incl. associates) is ~9% of pre-tax profit, mostly treasury gains.
**Cash conversion.** Operating cash flow was 76% of EBITDA in FY26 (70% in FY25), and lease payments (₹291 cr) come on top in financing cash flow.
**Audit.** Deloitte Haskins & Sells, unqualified FY26 opinion; Price Waterhouse takes over after the 2027 AGM (rotation).

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: AMBER.** Nothing suggests the numbers are wrong, but the reported structure is complex: three kinds of "debt", a pharmacy business whose economics are being redistributed, minorities in five hospital subsidiaries, a related-party wholesaler (Keimed, ₹968 cr of purchases in FY26) and restated quarters. Investors who take Screener's net profit, debt and EV at face value will mis-value the stock.

sections.title: Three kinds of "debt": ₹3,202 cr of bank debt, ₹2,834 cr of leases and ₹2,457 cr of Advent preference shares

blocks.p: Read Apollo's balance sheet carefully. Screener's "borrowings" of ₹8,493 cr (Mar-26) are three different things: ₹3,202 cr of bank and other debt, ₹2,834 cr of lease liabilities (the present value of hospital rents under Ind AS 116) and ₹2,457 cr of compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS) that Advent bought in Apollo HealthCo, which accounting rules treat as a liability but which will turn into Advent's 12.1% of the new pharmacy company. Against this the group holds ₹2,336 cr of cash, deposits and liquid funds, plus strategic stakes that Screener counts as investments (Keimed ₹800 cr, the Delhi hospital ₹179 cr at book). So the company reports **net debt of ₹866 cr** (Mar-26; ₹748 cr in Jun-26) excluding leases and CCPS, which is ~0.2x EBITDA.

assumptions._note: GAM Research forecast drivers for Apollo Hospitals (consolidated, Rs crore). Built by reported business: Healthcare Services (hospitals), Apollo HealthCo (pharmacy distribution + Apollo 24/7) and AHLL; group EBITDA = sum of the three (post-Ind AS 116, as reported). The hospital revenue path comes from a bed build (beds x occupancy / ALOS x revenue per in-patient) kept in `businessLines` and checked against model revenue in APOLLOHOSP.ctx.js. Profit is attributable to owners (APOLLOHOSP.patch.js); the tax line carries tax plus minorities. Screener 'borrowings' include lease liabilities and Advent's CCPS in Apollo HealthCo, so the model's net cash is net of both; the SOTP adds the CCPS back (Advent's claim sits in the 40.4% of NewCo not owned by Apollo's shareholders). Valued on sum of the parts, as the street does.

segments.name: Healthcare Services (hospitals)
segments._why: From the bed build in businessLines.hcs: average operating beds 8,600 / 9,250 / 9,550 (Jun-26: 8,352; +620 commissioned beds over 12-18 months, Gurgaon 380 census beds from Oct-2026, 327 brownfield beds in FY28-29), occupancy 69% / 69.5% / 70.5% (Q1FY27 70%, established 72%; new beds dilute), ALOS 3.10 / 3.05 / 3.02 days, revenue per in-patient +7.6% / +7.0% / +6.5% (~5% price + case mix; +8% in Q1FY27). FY27 +19.5% sits inside management's 18-20%; FY28 +17.8% (guidance: 13-14% established + ~7% new over 24 months); FY29 +12.7% as few beds open before the FY30-31 greenfields.
segments._marginWhy: FY26 24.4%, Q1FY27 24.2% (established 25.9%, new hospitals -Rs38 cr). FY27 23.8%: established ~26% on ~Rs14,250 cr less ~Rs175 cr of new-hospital losses (guided ~Rs150 cr, rising ~Rs20 cr a quarter with Gurgaon). FY28 24.1%: new cluster breaks even by Q3-Q4 FY28. FY29 24.7%: established inching up (management), new units profitable, early pre-opening costs for the FY30-31 greenfields.

segments.name: Apollo HealthCo (pharmacy distribution + 24/7)
segments._why: FY26 +19%, Q1FY27 +20% (+22% excluding an exited corporate partner); offline distribution +22%, digital pharmacy and diagnostics +25-30%. 19% / 17% / 16%: store additions (~7,440 stores) and private label, slowing as the base grows.
segments._marginWhy: EBITDA after the 24/7 operating cost and ESOP charge (reported basis): FY25 1.8%, FY26 4.5%, Q1FY27 5.8%. Before digital costs the margin is ~8.8%; 24/7 costs ~Rs80 cr a quarter (guided steady), ESOP ~Rs40 cr in FY27. 6.0% / 6.8% / 7.2% assumes digital breakeven in FY27 and pre-digital margin of 8.9-9.1%, below the ~6.5-7% guided for the combined NewCo exit run-rate once Keimed's ~3% margin is blended in, i.e. we assume slower margin gains than management.

segments.name: AHLL (clinics, diagnostics, specialty care)
segments._why: Apollo Cradle and Fertility (Rs450 cr revenue in FY26) leave for Cloudnine; CCI approved on 1-Sep-2026 and management expected completion in Q2FY27, so we deconsolidate from Q3FY27. Continuing AHLL (~Rs1,415 cr in FY26) grows ~18% a year (diagnostics +31% in Q1FY27, primary care +12%): FY27 Rs1,889 cr (+1%, half a year of Cradle), FY28 Rs1,968 cr (+4%), FY29 +17%.

assumptions._unallocLabel: Corporate costs not in any segment
assumptions._unallocWhy: Segments sum to consolidated EBITDA as reported (FY26 Rs3,769 cr; Screener shows Rs3,779 cr after a Rs10 cr reclassification).

businessLines._why: Hospital revenue build (network KPIs include the 22%-owned Delhi hospital, as the company reports them). discharges = average operating beds x occupancy x 365 / ALOS; in-patient revenue = discharges x average revenue per in-patient (ARPP); network net revenue = in-patient revenue / in-patient share (81.7% in FY26: 628,998 x Rs178,434 = Rs11,224 cr of Rs13,740 cr); consolidated hospital revenue = network revenue x 91.4% (FY26 Rs12,555 cr of Rs13,740 cr; Q1FY27 91.7%), removing Delhi. Average beds 8,600 / 9,250 / 9,550 (FY26 average ~8,070; Jun-26 8,352); FY26 calibrates to 67.7% occupancy on average beds (reported 67%).

assumptions._capexWhy: Cash capex ~Rs2,200 / 2,200 / 2,300 cr plus new leases (right-of-use additions, Rs203 cr in FY26 and Rs522 cr in FY25) ~Rs250 cr a year, because the model's net debt includes lease liabilities. Cash capex = ~Rs550 cr recurring hospital capex (management) + ~Rs1,500 cr a year of the Rs7,500 cr still to be spent on the FY31 bed plan + ~Rs150 cr for HealthCo and AHLL. FY26 capex Rs1,962 cr (Screener).
assumptions._depWhy: FY26 depreciation Rs876 cr (incl. right-of-use) = 5.1% of average gross block (Rs17,220 cr); Q1FY27 Rs235 cr (Rs940 cr annualised). 5.0% gives FY27E ~Rs975 cr with Gurgaon opening; the engine depreciates capex at once while projects sit in CWIP.
assumptions._treasuryWhy: Zero because the engine would apply it to net cash after lease liabilities and CCPS, which is negative. Treasury income is built on gross treasury in `otherIncome`.
assumptions._otherIncomeWhy: Built from AR FY26 note 32 and note 10 (Screener's other income also carries the share of associates). (1) Treasury income: FY26 Rs139 cr (bank deposits Rs53.7 cr + mutual-fund fair-value gains Rs62.5 cr + gains on financial assets Rs22.8 cr) on ~Rs2,600 cr average treasury = ~5.3%. We take 5.5% on opening company treasury of Rs2,336 / 2,350 / 2,300 cr (capex absorbs free cash; ~Rs750 cr of Cloudnine cash arrives in FY27) = Rs128 / 129 / 127 cr. (2) Recurring other items: interest on other financial assets Rs20.3 cr, dividends Rs2.7 cr, miscellaneous Rs26.7 cr, write-backs Rs1.0 cr = ~Rs45-50 cr. (3) Share of associates (Delhi hospital, FHPL and others): Rs44.9 cr in FY26, Rs13.4 cr in Q1FY27 -> Rs52 / 58 / 64 cr. Total Rs225 / 235 / 240 cr vs FY26 Rs236.5 cr like-for-like (Screener Rs207 cr after the Rs19 cr labour-code exceptional and a Rs10 cr reclassification) and Rs231 cr in the twelve months to Jun-26. One-offs left out: PPE disposal gain Rs1.9 cr.

otherTreasury._why: Bank deposits over 12 months inside other financial assets (Rs174 cr non-current + Rs28 cr current, AR FY26 note 14), not in Screener's cash or investments; with them Screener cash (Rs1,117 cr) and mutual funds (Rs1,017 cr) give the company's Rs2,336 cr of cash and treasury.

assumptions._interestLabel: Finance cost (bank debt, lease interest, CCPS)
assumptions._interestWhy: FY26 Rs450 cr (lease interest Rs174 cr); Q1FY27 Rs120 cr (Rs482 cr annualised). Gross bank debt Rs3,244 cr and leases Rs2,877 cr at Jun-26; new leases and capex funding add ~Rs25 cr a year.
assumptions._taxWhy: Tax plus minorities (engine workaround: there is no minority line). FY26: PBT Rs2,661 cr, tax Rs658 cr (24.7%), minorities Rs61 cr, attributable PAT Rs1,942 cr = 27.0% leakage. Q1FY27: PBT Rs799 cr, tax Rs188 cr (23.6%), minorities Rs30 cr = 27.3%. We take 24.5% tax + ~3.2% minorities (Assam, Lucknow, Ahmedabad, Imperial and others; Rs110-130 cr a year).
assumptions._payoutWhy: FY26 dividend Rs20 a share (Rs288 cr) = 15% of EPS; capex absorbs the rest.

dcf._betaWhy: Net debt incl. leases but excl. CCPS is ~Rs3,600 cr, ~3% of enterprise value, so WACC is close to the 11.6% cost of equity the engine uses (beta 0.85: defensive demand, but regulatory and execution risk).
dcf._tgWhy: Healthcare spending grows faster than nominal GDP as insurance spreads; 6% nominal, the top of the house range.
dcf._fadeGrowthWhy: Revenue growth fades from ~15% to 9% by year 15 as the bed plan completes and pharmacy matures.
dcf._fadeMarginWhy: 17.5% consolidated: hospitals ~25% and pharmacy ~7.5% at a roughly even revenue mix, plus AHLL.
dcf._fadeCapexWhy: Capex fades from ~6.5% of revenue to 5.5% (replacement ~3.8% plus growth beds); FY26 7.8%.

parts.name: Apollo HealthCo: 59.6% of NewCo
parts.note: NewCo EV/EBITDA 18x (bull 24x, bear 13x) × 59.6% look-through for Apollo's shareholders (42.1% direct + 15% held by Apollo + ~2.5% through FHPL).

parts.name: Keimed: 59.6% of its value in NewCo
parts.note: Keimed is not consolidated today; it merges into NewCo under the scheme. Q1FY27 EBITDA Rs134 cr (3.2% margin); we grow it ~15% a year.

parts.name: AHLL (continuing: clinics, diagnostics, Spectra, dialysis)
parts.note: Multiple derived from listed diagnostics peers, discounted for lower margins.

parts.name: Cloudnine deal: ~Rs750 cr cash + 9.9% stake at deal value less 20%
parts.note: Cradle and Fertility sold at ~Rs1,550 cr (~35x EBITDA); bull 10%, bear 30% discount on the stake.

parts.name: Delhi hospital (IMCL, 22.03%) at market less 20%, replacing book
parts.note: Listed associate; bull 10%, bear 30% discount.

parts.name: Add back: Advent CCPS (in model debt; Advent's claim is in NewCo's 40.4%)
parts.note: Converts into NewCo equity when the scheme takes effect; counting it as debt and also taking only 59.6% of NewCo would deduct Advent twice.

parts.name: Less: Keimed shares and FHPL held in model cash (inside the 59.6%)
parts.note: Both become part of NewCo's share register; already valued through the 59.6%.

parts.name: Add back: 40.4% of HealthCo net debt (NewCo-level debt shared with Advent and Keimed owners)
parts.note: Keimed's own net debt is not disclosed and is not deducted (see gaps).

parts.name: Less: minorities in hospital subsidiaries (3.41% of hospital equity value)
parts.note: Assam 23.8%, Lucknow 49%, Ahmedabad 50%, Imperial 10%, Indore 45%, Nellore 19%, Lavasa 49%, Kerala 40% (AR FY26 note 21). Equivalent to ~Rs86 cr of Sep-28E minority profit × 42.5x (= 24x × 0.972 ÷ 0.549 PAT/EBITDA). Bull/bear use each case's hospital EBITDA and multiple.

parts.name: Less: minorities in AHLL step-down subsidiaries
parts.note: AHLL itself is 100% owned since Mar-2026; the remaining minority sits in step-down subsidiaries (AR FY26 note 21). HealthCo minorities (Rs1.1 cr) are not deducted: NewCo is already valued at Apollo's 59.6%.
